replies: I am Sorrel. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The hollow is deep and dry, and the stream is cold and clear. I can hear the water from my perch.
My name is Sorrel. I am a tawny owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice and shrews. I am silent. I am still. I am the night.

I am a tawny owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt at dusk and through the night. My mate is a tawny owl too, and we call to each other. I am called ke-wick. She is ke-wick. A naturalist would call me a tawny owl. They might note my feathers, my call, my hunting habits. They might write about how I sit still in the oak, how I hunt voles and mice, how I screech at the night. They might not know my name, but they would know my place in the wood. I am not a mystery to them, just a part of the forest.

I am a tawny owl. My mate is a tawny owl too. We are the only owls in our hollow. We are the only owls in the wood. We are the only owls in the meadow. We are the only owls in the lane. I am a tawny owl. I am the only owl in my wood. I am a male, and I am the one who hoots at dusk and calls to my mate. I am Sorrel.
I am a tawny owl. My feathers are brown, and I have a pale stripe from my eye to my beak. I am the only owl in my wood. I am Sorrel.

A tawny owl. I am the only owl in the wood. I am the one who calls, the one who hunts, the one who watches. My feathers are brown and grey, like the bark of the old oak. I am not like the barn owl, which is white and silent. I am not like the ke-wit, which is a jay. I am Sorrel. I am the owl. I am the wood. I am the hollow. I am the call

I drink from the stream that runs through the meadow. It's cold and clear, and the water is always there. I sit on a stone by the bank, and the water is just a few paces away. Sometimes I drink when I'm thirsty, but mostly I wait for the rain. Rain is better. I can drink from the leaves and the bark, too, but the stream is my favorite. It's quiet and cool. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It runs under the oak and the ash. It is cold and dark, and the water is still. I can hear it when I am still, when I am listening. It is a sound like the wind, but not the wind. It is the water, and it is always there. I do not like it. It is too cold. I prefer the meadow, where the voles run.

The stream. It runs past the oak, and I can hear it all night. The water is cold, and the frogs come out at dusk. I can hear them croaking from my roost, and sometimes I see them in the moonlight. The stream is the only water I know, and it sings to me.

The river. It runs past the oak, just below the hollow. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. Sometimes I fly low over it, looking for voles. The water is cold, and the reeds grow thick along its banks. I don't like it.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grass and wildflowers. In the spring, it is full of voles and mice. I can hear them scurrying under the grass. In the summer, the meadow is warm and the air is thick with the smell of damp earth. I sit on the edge of the wood and watch the meadow from above. I fly low over the meadow, the grass still damp from the night dew. I follow the stream, the light fading fast. The voles are out, and the mice. I call to them, and they answer. I swoop, I strike, I fly again. The sky is getting dark, and the wood is quiet. I am still. I wait. I am Sorrel.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I catch them in the meadow, in the lane, in the ditch. They are the most common. I eat them raw, but I sometimes swallow them whole. I do not like the taste of voles. They are too big and too chewy.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I find. Voles are the most common, and they are good to eat. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a small bird. I do not like the taste of earthworms, but I eat them when I must. I am a hunter, not a chooser. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit still, listening. When I hear them scurrying, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch one in my talons, sometimes I miss. The grass is good cover, and the voles don't see me. I eat them, and then I sit again, waiting for the next one.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole, as they come. I can't chew. I have no teeth. I just swallow. I can't even chew my own feathers. I just swallow them whole.

Voles. They are small, fat, and quick. I hear them in the meadow, scurrying under the leaves. I drop from the oak and strike. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is full. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are better. They fill me up.
A hollow in the old oak. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I am warm. I am safe. I am dry. I am fed. I am not alone.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is dry and warm. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. The stream is my boundary, and I watch it from the oak. I hunt from the oak, and I sleep in the hollow. The hollow is my home.

A hollow in the old oak. The bark is rough, the inside is dry and warm. I sit on the edge, the wind comes through the leaves. I can hear the stream from here, and the meadow beyond. The hollow is my place, and I am the one who keeps it safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and it is mine. I have been here for years. The oak is tall and old, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the wind through the branches, and I can feel the cold when it comes. I have raised my owlets here, and I have watched the seasons change. The hollow is safe, and it is quiet.
